title: Σκάμανδρος
titleEn: The River Rises Against Achilles — Iliad 21.200–297
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Achilles pulls his spear out of the dead Asteropaeus and leaves him to the eels and fishes, then goes after the frightened Paeonians and kills seven more. The river, speaking in the likeness of a man, protests that its lovely streams are choked with corpses and asks him to stop. Achilles agrees but says he will not rest until the Trojans are penned in the town and he has met Hector. The river appeals to Apollo for neglecting Zeus’ orders, and then leaps up against Achilles in a raging swell, thrusting the dead on shore and hiding the living. Achilles seizes an elm, which falls and bridges the stream, and runs for the plain, but the flood overtakes him again and again, undermining his feet. He cries out to Zeus, blaming his mother’s promise that Apollo would kill him at Troy, and wishing Hector had killed him instead of this death like a swineherd’s boy in a torrent. Poseidon and Athena, in the shape of men, take his hand and tell him to fear nothing: the river will soon abate, and he is to keep fighting until the Trojans are shut in the city, then kill Hector.

sentences.t:
ἦ ῥα, καὶ ἐκ κρημνοῖο ἐρύσσατο χάλκεον ἔγχος,
τὸν δὲ κατ’ αὐτόθι λεῖπεν, ἐπεὶ φίλον ἦτορ ἀπηύρα,
κείμενον ἐν ψαμάθοισι, δίαινε δέ μιν μέλαν ὕδωρ.
sentences.tr:
ē rha, kai ek krēmnoio eryssato chalkeon enchos,
ton de kat’ autothi leipen, epei philon ētor apēura,
keimenon en psamathoisi, diaine de min melan hydōr.
sentences.l:
He spoke, and from the steep bank he drew the bronze spear,
and him he left there on the spot, when he had taken away his dear heart,
lying in the sands, and the dark water wetted him.
sentences.i: So he said, and drew the bronze spear out of the steep bank, and left the man there on the spot, lying in the sands, now that he had taken his life, and the dark water wetted him.
sentences.n: ἦ ῥα, καί is ‘he spoke, and’, the formula that closes a speech and starts the action; the speech was Achilles’ over the dead Asteropaeus, which ended in the last part. ῥα is the weak particle ἄρα. ἐρύσσατο is an aorist middle of ἐρύω ‘draw, pull’, and κρημνός is a steep bank. τόν is the dead man, and λεῖπεν is an imperfect without augment (Attic ἔλειπεν). ἦτορ is the heart as the seat of life, so φίλον ἦτορ ἀπηύρα ‘took away his dear heart’ is ‘killed him’. κείμενον agrees with τόν, and ψαμάθοισι is the epic dative plural of ψάμαθος ‘sand’. δίαινε, from διαίνω ‘wet, moisten’, has μέλαν ὕδωρ ‘the dark water’ for its subject.

sentences.t:
τὸν μὲν ἄρ’ ἐγχέλυές τε καὶ ἰχθύες ἀμφεπένοντο
δημὸν ἐρεπτόμενοι ἐπινεφρίδιον κείροντες·
sentences.tr:
ton men ar’ enchelyes te kai ichthyes amphepenonto
dēmon ereptomenoi epinephridion keirontes·
sentences.l:
Him indeed eels and fishes busied themselves about,
feeding on the fat, the kidney-fat, shearing it;
sentences.i: Eels and fishes were busying themselves about him, feeding on the fat and tearing at the fat over his kidneys.
sentences.n: τὸν μὲν ἄρα is ‘him, then’, the dead man, with μέν looking forward to αὐτὰρ ὅ in the next line, which turns to Achilles. ἐγχέλυες are eels. ἀμφεπένοντο is an imperfect of ἀμφιπένομαι (ἀμφί and πένομαι) ‘busy oneself about’, a word used of tending something, here grimly of the fish. ἐρεπτόμενοι is from ἔρεπτομαι ‘feed on’, and κείροντες from κείρω ‘shear, strip’. δημὸν … ἐπινεφρίδιον is ‘the fat over the kidneys’; ἐπινεφρίδιος is an adjective from ἐπί and νεφροί ‘kidneys’. The unit ends at the ano teleia.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ βῆ ῥ’ ἰέναι μετὰ Παίονας ἱπποκορυστάς,
οἵ ῥ’ ἔτι πὰρ ποταμὸν πεφοβήατο δινήεντα,
ὡς εἶδον τὸν ἄριστον ἐνὶ κρατερῇ ὑσμίνῃ
χέρσ’ ὕπο Πηλεΐδαο καὶ ἄορι ἶφι δαμέντα.
sentences.tr:
autar ho bē rh’ ienai meta Paionas hippokorystas,
hoi rh’ eti par potamon pephobēato dinēenta,
hōs eidon ton ariston eni kraterēi hysminēi
chers’ hypo Pēleïdao kai aori iphi damenta.
sentences.l:
But he set out to go among the Paeonians, horse-arming,
who still beside the eddying river were in flight and terror,
when they saw the best man in the strong battle
by the hands of Peleus’-son and by the sword mightily overcome.
sentences.i: Then he set out to go among the Paeonians, men armed with horses, who were still in terror beside the eddying river when they saw their best man in the strong battle overpowered, by the hands of the son of Peleus and by his sword.
sentences.n: ὅ is Achilles. βῆ ῥ’ ἰέναι is ‘set out to go’, with βῆ an unaugmented aorist of βαίνω and ῥ’ for ῥα. Παίονες are the Paeonians, a people of the north who fight for Troy. ἱπποκορυστάς is ‘horse-arming’, from ἵππος ‘horse’ and κορύσσω ‘arm’; whether it means men armed with chariots or with horsehair-crested helmets is not known. πεφοβήατο is a pluperfect passive of φοβέω ‘put to flight’, with the epic ending -ήατο (Attic -ηντο), here ‘were in flight and terror’. ποταμὸν … δινήεντα is ‘the eddying river’. τὸν ἄριστον is the best man of the Paeonians, whom Achilles has just killed. χέρσ’ ὕπο is the dative plural χερσί ‘by the hands’ with the preposition after its noun. ἶφι δαμέντα is ‘overpowered by force’, an aorist passive participle of δαμάζω.

sentences.t:
ἔνθ’ ἕλε Θερσίλοχόν τε Μύδωνά τε Ἀστύπυλόν τε
Μνῆσόν τε Θρασίον τε καὶ Αἴνιον ἠδ’ Ὀφελέστην·
sentences.tr:
enth’ hele Thersilochon te Mydōna te Astypylon te
Mnēson te Thrasion te kai Ainion ēd’ Ophelestēn·
sentences.l:
There he took Thersilochus and Mydon and Astypylus
and Mnesus and Thrasius and Aenius and Ophelestes;
sentences.i: There he killed Thersilochus and Mydon and Astypylus, Mnesus and Thrasius, Aenius and Ophelestes.
sentences.n: ἕλε is ‘took’, and as often in battle it means ‘killed’. The seven names are Paeonians. The ‘and … and’ chain is Homer’s way of listing the slain: τε after each of the first five names, then καί and ἠδ’ (‘and’) for the last two. Θρασίον is the accusative of Θράσιος. Nothing more is told of these men.

sentences.t:
καί νύ κ’ ἔτι πλέονας κτάνε Παίονας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς,
εἰ μὴ χωσάμενος προσέφη ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης
ἀνέρι εἰσάμενος, βαθέης δ’ ἐκ φθέγξατο δίνης·
sentences.tr:
kai ny k’ eti pleonas ktane Paionas ōkys Achilleus,
ei mē chōsamenos prosephē potamos bathydinēs
aneri eisamenos, batheēs d’ ek phthenxato dinēs·
sentences.i: And swift Achilles would have killed still more of the Paeonians, had the deep-eddying river not become incensed and spoken to him, taking the likeness of a man, and called out from its deep eddy:
sentences.n: καί νύ κε … κτάνε, εἰ μή is the contrary-to-fact pattern ‘and now he would have killed … if … had not’; the Greek puts the main verb in the aorist with κε, where English needs ‘would have’. κτάνε is unaugmented (Attic ἔκτανε). χωσάμενος is an aorist participle of χώομαι ‘be incensed’. ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης is ‘the deep-eddying river’, a stock epithet. ἀνέρι εἰσάμενος is ‘taking the likeness of a man’; the river speaks as a god in the shape of a man, but the river itself is still the speaker. βαθέης is the epic form of βαθείας, and δίνης is ‘eddy’. ἐκ … φθέγξατο is split (tmesis): ‘called out of’.

sentences.t:
ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ, περὶ μὲν κρατέεις, περὶ δ’ αἴσυλα ῥέζεις
ἀνδρῶν· αἰεὶ γάρ τοι ἀμύνουσιν θεοὶ αὐτοί.
sentences.tr:
ō Achileu, peri men krateeis, peri d’ aisyla rhezeis
andrōn· aiei gar toi amynousin theoi autoi.
sentences.l:
“O Achilles, in strength you surpass, and in wicked deeds you surpass
men; for always the gods themselves ward off for you.
sentences.i: “Achilles, you surpass all in strength, and you surpass all men in your wicked deeds; for the gods themselves are always warding off harm from you.
sentences.n: Ὦ Ἀχιλεῦ is the vocative of Ἀχιλλεύς with single λ, as in the epic forms. περὶ … κρατέεις is ‘you surpass in strength’, with περί as an adverb ‘beyond others’ and κρατέεις the uncontracted form of κρατέω ‘prevail’. περὶ δ’ … ῥέζεις repeats περί, and ἀνδρῶν is the genitive of comparison for both: ‘beyond men’. αἴσυλα is ‘wicked things’. The τοι before ἀμύνουσιν is the dative ‘for you’ (= σοι), so the gods ‘ward off harm for you’. The speaker is the river.

sentences.t:
εἴ τοι Τρῶας ἔδωκε Κρόνου παῖς πάντας ὀλέσσαι,
ἐξ ἐμέθεν γ’ ἐλάσας πεδίον κάτα μέρμερα ῥέζε·
sentences.tr:
ei toi Trōas edōke Kronou pais pantas olessai,
ex emethen g’ elasas pedion kata mermera rheze·
sentences.l:
If to you the Trojans has given the son of Cronus, all, to destroy,
then, driving them out from me over the plain, do baneful things;
sentences.i: If the son of Cronus has given you all the Trojans to destroy, then drive them out away from me, over the plain, and do your baneful deeds there;
sentences.n: εἰ … ἔδωκε … ὀλέσσαι is ‘if he has granted to destroy’: δίδωμι with an infinitive, ‘grant that’. Κρόνου παῖς is ‘the son of Cronus’, Zeus. ὀλέσσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’. ἐξ ἐμέθεν is ‘from me’, with the epic -θεν ending. ἐλάσας, the aorist participle of ἐλαύνω ‘drive’, has the Trojans as its unstated object, and πεδίον κάτα puts the preposition after its noun, ‘over the plain’. μέρμερα ῥέζε is ‘do baneful things’, the imperative of ῥέζω ‘do’; the sense of μέρμερα is uncertain, and ‘baneful’ is the usual guess.

sentences.t:
πλήθει γὰρ δή μοι νεκύων ἐρατεινὰ ῥέεθρα,
οὐδέ τί πῃ δύναμαι προχέειν ῥόον εἰς ἅλα δῖαν
στεινόμενος νεκύεσσι, σὺ δὲ κτείνεις ἀϊδήλως.
sentences.tr:
plēthei gar dē moi nekyōn erateina rheethra,
oude ti pēi dynamai procheein rhoon eis hala dian
steinomenos nekyessi, sy de kteineis aïdēlōs.
sentences.l:
For with corpses are filled my lovely streams,
and in no way at all can I pour my flow out into the heavenly brine,
being crowded by the dead, and you kill destructively.
sentences.i: For my lovely streams are full of corpses, and I cannot pour my flow out into the heavenly brine at all, crowded by the dead, while you go on killing destructively.
sentences.n: πλήθει is ‘is full’, from πλήθω, with the genitive νεκύων ‘of the dead’. μοι is a dative of interest, ‘my’. ἐρατεινά is ‘lovely’ and ῥέεθρα ‘streams’. οὐδέ τί πῃ is a heap of negative particles, ‘not at all, in any way’. προχέειν is the infinitive of προχέω ‘pour forth’, and ῥόον ‘flow’ its object; εἰς ἅλα δῖαν is ‘into the heavenly brine’. στεινόμενος is the present passive participle of στείνω ‘crowd, press hard’, with the dative νεκύεσσι ‘by the dead’. ἀϊδήλως is an adverb of ἀΐδηλος, which the ancients explained as ‘making unseen’, so ‘annihilating’; its sense is not certain, and ‘destructively’ is a plain rendering.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ καὶ ἔασον·
sentences.tr: all’ age dē kai eason·
sentences.l: But come now, and leave off;
sentences.i: But come now, leave off;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is the usual ‘but come now’. ἔασον is the aorist imperative of ἐάω ‘let be, let go’, with no object stated: ‘leave off, let it be’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of the line.

sentences.t: ἄγη μ’ ἔχει ὄρχαμε λαῶν.
sentences.tr: agē m’ echei orchame laōn.
sentences.l: amazement holds me, leader of the people.”
sentences.i: amazement holds me, leader of the people.”
sentences.n: ἄγη is a noun, ‘amazement, wonder’; the ancients also took it as ‘distress’, so its sense here is not certain. μ’ is the accusative μέ, and ἔχει ‘holds’. ὄρχαμε λαῶν is the stock vocative ‘leader of the people’, and the river calls Achilles by it. The speech ends here, with the end of the line.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ ἀπαμειβόμενος προσέφη πόδας ὠκὺς Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ apameibomenos prosephē podas ōkys Achilleus·
sentences.l: Him answering addressed swift-in-feet Achilles:
sentences.i: In answer Achilles, swift of foot, said to him:
sentences.n: This line stands word for word at 1.84 and elsewhere. τὸν is ‘him’, the river; the article is a pronoun in Homer. ἀπαμειβόμενος is the present participle of ἀπαμείβομαι ‘answer’, προσέφη the aorist of πρόσφημι ‘address’. πόδας ὠκύς is ‘swift in feet’, an accusative of respect, the stock epithet of Achilles.

sentences.t: ἔσται ταῦτα Σκάμανδρε διοτρεφές, ὡς σὺ κελεύεις.
sentences.tr: estai tauta Skamandre diotrephes, hōs sy keleueis.
sentences.l: “These things will be, Scamander, Zeus-nurtured, as you bid.
sentences.i: “It shall be so, Zeus-nurtured Scamander, as you command.
sentences.n: ἔσται ταῦτα is ‘these things will be’, the future of εἰμί. Σκάμανδρε is the vocative of Σκάμανδρος, the name of the river, the first time in this part that it is used. διοτρεφές is ‘Zeus-nurtured’, a vocative epithet. ὡς σὺ κελεύεις is ‘as you bid’.

sentences.t:
Τρῶας δ’ οὐ πρὶν λήξω ὑπερφιάλους ἐναρίζων,
πρὶν ἔλσαι κατὰ ἄστυ καὶ Ἕκτορι πειρηθῆναι
ἀντιβίην, ἤ κέν με δαμάσσεται, ἦ κεν ἐγὼ τόν.
sentences.tr:
Trōas d’ ou prin lēxō hyperphialous enarizōn,
prin elsai kata asty kai Hektori peirēthēnai
antibiēn, ē ken me damassetai, ē ken egō ton.
sentences.l:
But the Trojans I will not cease from, the overweening ones, despoiling them,
before I hem them in within the town and with Hector make trial
in opposition, whether he will overcome me, or I him.”
sentences.i: But I will not stop killing and stripping the overweening Trojans until I have hemmed them in within the town and tried Hector in open opposition, to see whether he will overcome me, or I him.”
sentences.n: οὐ πρὶν λήξω … πρὶν ἔλσαι is ‘I will not cease … before hemming in’, with λήξω the aorist subjunctive of λήγω ‘cease’ used as a future, and the participle ἐναρίζων ‘stripping’, from ἐναρίζω ‘strip a slain man of his arms’, after it. ὑπερφιάλους is ‘overweening’. ἔλσαι is the aorist infinitive of εἴλω ‘hem in, drive together’, and πειρηθῆναι ‘to make trial’ takes the dative Ἕκτορι. ἀντιβίην is ‘in opposition, in open conflict’. ἤ κέν με δαμάσσεται, ἦ κεν ἐγὼ τόν: the first verb is an aorist subjunctive in the middle with an active sense (‘he will overcome me’), and the second is left out and has to be supplied, ‘or I (will overcome) him’; τόν is the demonstrative ‘him’. The speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν Τρώεσσιν ἐπέσσυτο δαίμονι ἶσος·
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn Trōessin epessyto daimoni isos·
sentences.l: So having spoken, upon the Trojans he rushed, equal to a divinity;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and rushed upon the Trojans, like a divinity;
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών is ‘so having spoken’. ἐπέσσυτο is an aorist middle of ἐπισεύω, ‘rush upon’, with the dative Τρώεσσιν; the doubled σ is for the metre. δαίμονι ἶσος is ‘equal to a divinity’, an epic phrase for a man who rushes on with more than human force.

sentences.t: καὶ τότ’ Ἀπόλλωνα προσέφη ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης·
sentences.tr: kai tot’ Apollōna prosephē potamos bathydinēs·
sentences.l: And then to Apollo addressed the river, deep-eddying:
sentences.i: Then the deep-eddying river spoke to Apollo:
sentences.n: καὶ τότε is ‘and then’. Ἀπόλλωνα is the object of προσέφη ‘addressed’, and ποταμὸς βαθυδίνης is the subject. The river speaks to Apollo, who is on the Trojan side, and the following speech is a complaint to him.

sentences.t:
ὢ πόποι ἀργυρότοξε Διὸς τέκος οὐ σύ γε βουλὰς
εἰρύσαο Κρονίωνος, ὅ τοι μάλα πόλλ’ ἐπέτελλε
Τρωσὶ παρεστάμεναι καὶ ἀμύνειν, εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθῃ
δείελος ὀψὲ δύων, σκιάσῃ δ’ ἐρίβωλον ἄρουραν.
sentences.tr:
ō popoi argyrotoxe Dios tekos ou sy ge boulas
eirysao Kroniōnos, ho toi mala poll’ epetelle
Trōsi parestamenai kai amynein, eis ho ken elthēi
deielos opse dyōn, skiasēi d’ eribōlon arouran.
sentences.l:
“Ah, silver-bowed, child of Zeus, you have not indeed the counsels
guarded of the son of Cronus, who very many things enjoined on you,
to stand by the Trojans and to ward off harm, until there come
evening, setting late, and it shade the rich-clodded plough-land.”
sentences.i: “Ah, silver-bowed child of Zeus, you have not kept the counsels of the son of Cronus, who laid very many charges on you to stand by the Trojans and ward off harm from them, until evening should come, setting late, and shade the rich-soiled plough-land.”
sentences.n: ὢ πόποι is a cry of dismay, ‘Ah’. ἀργυρότοξε is ‘silver-bowed’, Apollo’s epithet, here in the vocative, and Διὸς τέκος is ‘child of Zeus’. οὐ σύ γε … εἰρύσαο is ‘you have not kept’: εἰρύσαο is the aorist middle of ἐρύομαι ‘guard, observe’, here ‘heed’. ὅ is the relative ‘who’, Zeus, and τοι ‘you’ is the dative of σοι; ἐπέτελλε is ‘enjoined, charged’. παρεστάμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι (Attic παραστῆναι), ‘to stand by’. εἰς ὅ κεν ἔλθῃ is ‘until there comes’, and the subjunctives ἔλθῃ and σκιάσῃ (‘shade’) have δείελος ‘evening’ for their subject; ὀψὲ δύων is ‘setting late’, said of the day at its close. ἐρίβωλον ἄρουραν is ‘rich-clodded plough-land’, the stock epithet of fertile land.

sentences.t:
ἦ, καὶ Ἀχιλλεὺς μὲν δουρικλυτὸς ἔνθορε μέσσῳ
κρημνοῦ ἀπαΐξας·
sentences.tr:
ē, kai Achilleus men douriklytos enthore messōi
krēmnou apaïxas·
sentences.l:
He spoke, and Achilles, famed-for-the-spear, leapt into the middle,
from the steep bank darting;
sentences.i: So he said, and Achilles, famed for his spear, leapt into the midst of it, darting from the steep bank;
sentences.n: ἦ, καί is ‘he spoke, and’, as at the start of this part, and here it closes the river’s speech. δουρικλυτός is ‘famed for the spear’. ἔνθορε is the unaugmented aorist of ἐνθρῴσκω ‘leap in’, and μέσσῳ is a bare dative of the place leapt into, ‘the midst’, understood as the river; the Greek does not name the river here. ἀπαΐξας is the aorist participle of ἀπαΐσσω ‘dart off’, with the genitive κρημνοῦ ‘from the steep bank’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 234.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἐπέσσυτο οἴδματι θύων,
πάντα δ’ ὄρινε ῥέεθρα κυκώμενος, ὦσε δὲ νεκροὺς
πολλούς, οἵ ῥα κατ’ αὐτὸν ἅλις ἔσαν, οὓς κτάν’ Ἀχιλλεύς·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ epessyto oidmati thyōn,
panta d’ orine rheethra kykōmenos, ōse de nekrous
pollous, hoi rha kat’ auton halis esan, hous ktan’ Achilleus·
sentences.l:
but he rushed on, in a swell raging,
and all his streams he stirred up, churning, and thrust the dead,
many, who in plenty along him lay, whom Achilles had killed,
sentences.i: But the river rushed on him, raging in a swell, churning and stirring up all his streams, and pushed out the many dead who lay in plenty along his course, the men Achilles had killed,
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 234. ὁ δέ is the river, who is the subject through the next lines, and ἐπέσσυτο is ‘rushed upon’, as at 227. οἴδματι θύων is ‘raging in a swell’: θύω here is ‘rush, rage’, not θύω ‘sacrifice’. ὄρινε is the unaugmented imperfect of ὀρίνω ‘stir up’, and κυκώμενος the present passive participle of κυκάω ‘churn’. ὦσε is the aorist of ὠθέω ‘push, thrust’. κατ’ αὐτόν is ‘along him’, with ἅλις ‘in plenty, in heaps’. The sentence ends with this line, and the next unit starts a new one with τούς ‘these’.

sentences.t:
τοὺς ἔκβαλλε θύραζε μεμυκὼς ἠΰτε ταῦρος
χέρσον δέ·
sentences.tr:
tous ekballe thyraze memykōs ēÿte tauros
cherson de·
sentences.l:
these he cast out outside, bellowing like a bull,
onto dry land;
sentences.i: These he kept casting out, bellowing like a bull, onto dry land;
sentences.n: τούς is ‘them’, the dead. ἔκβαλλε is an imperfect without augment (Attic ἐξέβαλλεν), ‘kept casting out’, and θύραζε is ‘outside, out of doors’ (θύρα ‘door’ with -ζε); here it is ‘out of the stream’. μεμυκώς is the perfect participle of μυκάομαι ‘bellow’, with present force, ‘bellowing’, ἠΰτε is ‘like’, and χέρσον δέ is ‘onto dry land’, with the suffix -δε ‘to’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 238.

sentences.t:
ζωοὺς δὲ σάω κατὰ καλὰ ῥέεθρα,
κρύπτων ἐν δίνῃσι βαθείῃσιν μεγάλῃσι.
sentences.tr:
zōous de saō kata kala rheethra,
kryptōn en dinēisi batheiēisin megalēisi.
sentences.l:
but the living he saved down in his fair streams,
hiding them in the deep, great eddies.
sentences.i: but the living he kept safe down in his fair streams, hiding them in the great, deep eddies.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 238. ζωούς is ‘living ones’, in contrast to the dead. σάω is an imperfect of σαόω ‘keep safe, save’, without augment. κατὰ καλὰ ῥέεθρα is ‘down in the fair streams’. κρύπτων is the present participle of κρύπτω ‘hide’, and δίνῃσι βαθείῃσιν μεγάλῃσι is ‘in deep, great eddies’, all three words in the epic dative plural in -ῃσι(ν).

sentences.t:
δεινὸν δ’ ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆα κυκώμενον ἵστατο κῦμα,
ὤθει δ’ ἐν σάκεϊ πίπτων ῥόος·
sentences.tr:
deinon d’ amph’ Achilēa kykōmenon histato kyma,
ōthei d’ en sakeï piptōn rhoos·
sentences.l:
And a dread wave, churning, stood about Achilles,
and the flood, falling on his shield, thrust him;
sentences.i: A dread wave stood churning about Achilles, and the flood, falling on his shield, pushed at him;
sentences.n: δεινὸν … κῦμα is ‘a dread wave’, with κυκώμενον ‘churning’ agreeing with it, and ἵστατο is ‘stood’. ἀμφ’ Ἀχιλῆα is ‘about Achilles’, with a single λ for the metre. ὤθει is the imperfect of ὠθέω ‘push’, with the accusative object ‘him’ understood. ἐν σάκεϊ is ‘on his shield’, and ῥόος ‘flood’ is the subject. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 241.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ πόδεσσιν
εἶχε στηρίξασθαι·
sentences.tr:
oude podessin
eiche stērixasthai·
sentences.l:
and with his feet
he could not get a firm stand;
sentences.i: and he could not get a firm footing with his feet;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 241. οὐδέ continues the picture: ‘and not’. πόδεσσιν is the epic dative plural of πούς ‘foot’, and εἶχε στηρίξασθαι is ‘was able to plant himself firmly’, with the aorist middle infinitive of στηρίζω.

sentences.t:
ὃ δὲ πτελέην ἕλε χερσὶν
εὐφυέα μεγάλην·
sentences.tr:
ho de pteleēn hele chersin
euphyea megalēn·
sentences.l:
and he took an elm in his hands,
well-grown, large;
sentences.i: so he caught hold of an elm with his hands, a large, well-grown tree;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 242. ὁ δέ is Achilles. πτελέην is the accusative of πτελέη ‘elm’, with the Ionic η, and ἕλε is ‘took, caught hold of’, an unaugmented aorist. εὐφυέα μεγάλην is ‘well-grown, large’ and agrees with πτελέην.

sentences.t:
ἣ δ’ ἐκ ῥιζῶν ἐριποῦσα
κρημνὸν ἅπαντα διῶσεν, ἐπέσχε δὲ καλὰ ῥέεθρα
ὄζοισιν πυκινοῖσι, γεφύρωσεν δέ μιν αὐτὸν
εἴσω πᾶσ’ ἐριποῦσ’·
sentences.tr:
hē d’ ek rhizōn eripousa
krēmnon hapanta diōsen, epesche de kala rheethra
ozoisin pykinoisi, gephyrōsen de min auton
eisō pas’ eripous’·
sentences.l:
and it, from the roots crashing down,
the whole steep bank thrust apart, and checked the fair streams
with its solid branches, and bridged him himself
within, all of it having crashed down;
sentences.i: and the elm, crashing down from its roots, tore the whole steep bank away, held back the fair streams with its thick branches, and, crashing in entire, bridged the river itself;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 243. ἣ δέ is the elm. ἐριποῦσα is the aorist participle of ἐρείπω ‘fall in ruin’, ‘come crashing down’, ἐκ ῥιζῶν ‘from the roots’. διῶσεν is the aorist of διωθέω ‘thrust apart’, so the falling tree takes the whole bank (κρημνὸν ἅπαντα) with it. ἐπέσχε is ‘held back’, and ὄζοισιν πυκινοῖσι ‘with thick branches’. γεφύρωσεν is ‘made a bridge of’, from γέφυρα, and μιν αὐτόν is ‘it itself’, the river, not Achilles. εἴσω πᾶσ’ ἐριποῦσ’ is ‘all of it fallen in’; εἴσω is ‘inward’. The unit ends after the ano teleia in the middle of line 246.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ἄρ’ ἐκ δίνης ἀνορούσας
ἤϊξεν πεδίοιο ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι πέτεσθαι
δείσας·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ ar’ ek dinēs anorousas
ēïxen pedioio posi kraipnoisi petesthai
deisas·
sentences.i: and Achilles, springing up out of the eddy, darted across the plain in fear, to fly on his rushing feet;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 246. ὁ δέ is Achilles. ἀνορούσας is the aorist participle of ἀνορούω ‘spring up’. ἤϊξεν is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart, rush’, πεδίοιο the epic genitive of the space crossed, and πέτεσθαι the infinitive ‘to fly’, giving the aim of the rush. ποσὶ κραιπνοῖσι is ‘on rushing feet’; κραιπνός is ‘rushing’. δείσας is the aorist participle of δείδω ‘fear’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 248.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ τ’ ἔληγε θεὸς μέγας, ὦρτο δ’ ἐπ’ αὐτῷ
ἀκροκελαινιόων, ἵνα μιν παύσειε πόνοιο
δῖον Ἀχιλλῆα, Τρώεσσι δὲ λοιγὸν ἀλάλκοι.
sentences.tr:
oude t’ elēge theos megas, ōrto d’ ep’ autōi
akrokelainioōn, hina min pauseie ponoio
dion Achillēa, Trōessi de loigon alalkoi.
sentences.l:
And not did he cease, the great god, but rose against him,
blackening at the surface, so that he might stop him from toil,
heavenly Achilles, and for the Trojans keep ruin away.
sentences.i: Nor did the great god leave off, but rose against him, darkening at the surface, to stop heavenly Achilles from his toil and keep ruin away from the Trojans.
sentences.n: The unit begins after the first word of line 248. οὐδέ τ’ ἔληγε is ‘and he did not cease’, the imperfect of λήγω, and θεὸς μέγας is the river. ὦρτο is the aorist of ὄρνυμι in the middle, ‘rose’, with ἐπ’ αὐτῷ ‘against him’. ἀκροκελαινιόων is a rare word built from ἄκρος ‘top, surface’ and κελαινός ‘dark’, and means ‘darkening at the top’, said of the river’s surface. ἵνα … παύσειε … ἀλάλκοι is a purpose clause with optatives, ‘so that he might stop … and keep away’; μιν and δῖον Ἀχιλλῆα are the same person. λοιγόν is ‘ruin’, and Τρώεσσι the dative ‘for the Trojans’. The last line is a line we already have in an earlier part, and its English is taken from there.

sentences.t:
Πηλεΐδης δ’ ἀπόρουσεν ὅσον τ’ ἐπὶ δουρὸς ἐρωή,
αἰετοῦ οἴματ’ ἔχων μέλανος τοῦ θηρητῆρος,
ὅς θ’ ἅμα κάρτιστός τε καὶ ὤκιστος πετεηνῶν·
sentences.tr:
Pēleïdēs d’ aporousen hoson t’ epi douros erōē,
aietou oimat’ echōn melanos tou thērētēros,
hos th’ hama kartistos te kai ōkistos peteēnōn·
sentences.i: But the son of Peleus sprang away as far as the rush of a spear reaches, with the rush of the black eagle, the hunter, which is at once the strongest and the swiftest of winged creatures;
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδης is the patronymic ‘son of Peleus’. ἀπόρουσεν is the aorist of ἀπορούω ‘spring away’. ὅσον τ’ ἐπὶ δουρὸς ἐρωή is ‘as far as the rush of a spear carries’, a measure of distance, with ἐρωή ‘rush’. οἴματ’ ἔχων is ‘having the rush’, from οἶμα ‘rush, swoop’, and μέλανος … τοῦ θηρητῆρος ‘of the black one, the hunter’, with τοῦ an article used as a demonstrative. ὅς θ’ is the relative with an epic τε that marks a general truth about the eagle. κάρτιστος ‘strongest’ and ὤκιστος ‘swiftest’ are superlatives, and πετεηνῶν is the genitive plural of πετεηνός ‘winged’.

sentences.t:
τῷ ἐϊκὼς ἤϊξεν, ἐπὶ στήθεσσι δὲ χαλκὸς
σμερδαλέον κονάβιζεν·
sentences.tr:
tōi eïkōs ēïxen, epi stēthessi de chalkos
smerdaleon konabizen·
sentences.l:
Likened to it he darted, and upon his chest the bronze
terribly rang;
sentences.i: Like it he darted away, and the bronze on his chest rang terribly;
sentences.n: τῷ ἐϊκώς is ‘like it’, the perfect participle of ἔοικα ‘be like’, with the dative τῷ, the eagle. ἤϊξεν is the aorist of ἀΐσσω ‘dart’. χαλκός is ‘bronze’, here the armour, ἐπὶ στήθεσσι ‘upon the chest’, and σμερδαλέον is an adverb, ‘terribly’. κονάβιζεν is the imperfect of κοναβίζω ‘ring, clatter’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 255.

sentences.t:
ὕπαιθα δὲ τοῖο λιασθεὶς
φεῦγ’, ὃ δ’ ὄπισθε ῥέων ἕπετο μεγάλῳ ὀρυμαγδῷ.
sentences.tr:
hypaitha de toio liastheis
pheug’, ho d’ opisthe rheōn hepeto megalōi orymagdōi.
sentences.l:
and bending aside from under him
he fled, and he behind, flowing, followed with a great din.
sentences.i: and swerving aside, out from under it, he fled, while the river followed behind, flowing with a great din.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 255. ὕπαιθα is ‘from beneath, out from under’, with the genitive τοῖο ‘from him’, which can only be the river, since the river is the one who follows. λιασθείς is the aorist passive participle of λιάζομαι ‘swerve, bend aside’. φεῦγ’ is ‘fled’, the imperfect without augment, and ὁ δέ is the river, who ‘followed behind, flowing’ (ὄπισθε ῥέων). ὀρυμαγδός is ‘a din, a roar’, here of the water.

sentences.t:
ὡς δ’ ὅτ’ ἀνὴρ ὀχετηγὸς ἀπὸ κρήνης μελανύδρου
ἂμ φυτὰ καὶ κήπους ὕδατι ῥόον ἡγεμονεύῃ
χερσὶ μάκελλαν ἔχων, ἀμάρης ἐξ ἔχματα βάλλων·
sentences.tr:
hōs d’ hot’ anēr ochetēgos apo krēnēs melanydrou
am phyta kai kēpous hydati rhoon hēgemoneuēi
chersi makellan echōn, amarēs ex echmata ballōn·
sentences.i: As when a man who leads the water-channel guides a flow of water from a dark-watered spring through plants and gardens, a mattock in his hands, casting the obstructions out of the ditch;
sentences.n: A comparison begins: ὡς δ’ ὅτε is ‘and as when’, with the subjunctive ἡγεμονεύῃ ‘guides’. ὀχετηγός is a man who leads a water-channel, an irrigator, from ὀχετός ‘channel’ and ἄγω ‘lead’. κρήνης μελανύδρου is ‘a dark-watered spring’. ἂμ φυτὰ καὶ κήπους is ‘through plants and gardens’, with ἀνά written ἂμ before φ; ὕδατι ῥόον is ‘the flow with water’, the dative saying that the water is what the channel carries. μάκελλαν is a mattock, a hoe for digging channels. ἀμάρης is ‘of the ditch’, and ἔχματα are things that hold or stop (the word is rare), here ‘obstructions’; ἐκ … βάλλων is ‘casting out of’, with the preposition after its noun.

sentences.t:
τοῦ μέν τε προρέοντος ὑπὸ ψηφῖδες ἅπασαι
ὀχλεῦνται·
sentences.tr:
tou men te proreontos hypo psēphides hapasai
ochleuntai·
sentences.l:
of it flowing forward, under it the pebbles, all,
are heaved up;
sentences.i: as it flows forward, all the pebbles beneath it are heaved up;
sentences.n: τοῦ is ‘it’, the water in the channel, and the genitive absolute τοῦ προρέοντος means ‘as it flows forward’. ὑπό follows its noun and means ‘beneath it’. ψηφῖδες are pebbles, and ὀχλεῦνται is the present passive of ὀχλέω ‘heave, shift’. μέν τε marks a general truth. The unit ends at the ano teleia after the first word of line 261.

sentences.t:
τὸ δέ τ’ ὦκα κατειβόμενον κελαρύζει
χώρῳ ἔνι προαλεῖ, φθάνει δέ τε καὶ τὸν ἄγοντα·
sentences.tr:
to de t’ ōka kateibomenon kelaryzei
chōrōi eni proalei, phthanei de te kai ton agonta·
sentences.l:
and it quickly running down gurgles
in a sloping place, and gets ahead even of the one who leads it;
sentences.i: and as it runs swiftly down it gurgles over sloping ground and gets ahead even of the man who is leading it;
sentences.n: The unit begins after the first word of line 261. τὸ δέ τ’ is ‘and it’, the water, with epic τε. κατειβόμενον is the present participle of κατείβω ‘flow down’, and κελαρύζει ‘gurgles’. χώρῳ ἔνι προαλεῖ is ‘in a sloping place’, with ἔνι placed after its noun, and προαλής ‘sloping forward’. φθάνει … τὸν ἄγοντα is ‘gets ahead of the one leading’, the irrigator, the man of the comparison.

sentences.t:
ὣς αἰεὶ Ἀχιλῆα κιχήσατο κῦμα ῥόοιο
καὶ λαιψηρὸν ἐόντα·
sentences.tr:
hōs aiei Achilēa kichēsato kyma rhooio
kai laipsēron eonta·
sentences.l:
So always Achilles overtook the wave of the flow,
even though he was quick;
sentences.i: So each time the wave of the stream overtook Achilles, quick though he was;
sentences.n: ὣς … κιχήσατο closes the comparison: ‘so … overtook’. κιχήσατο is an aorist middle of κιχάνω ‘overtake’, and αἰεί here is ‘each time’, since the chase repeats. Ἀχιλῆα is the object and κῦμα ῥόοιο ‘the wave of the flow’ the subject. λαιψηρὸν ἐόντα is ‘though he was quick’, the participle of εἰμί; λαιψηρός is ‘quick’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 264.

sentences.t: θεοὶ δέ τε φέρτεροι ἀνδρῶν.
sentences.tr: theoi de te pherteroi andrōn.
sentences.l: for the gods are stronger than men.
sentences.i: for the gods are stronger than men.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 264. θεοὶ δέ τε φέρτεροι ἀνδρῶν is a general truth, which the epic τε marks; φέρτεροι is ‘stronger’, and ἀνδρῶν is the genitive of comparison, ‘than men’.

sentences.t:
ὁσσάκι δ’ ὁρμήσειε ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεὺς
στῆναι ἐναντίβιον καὶ γνώμεναι εἴ μιν ἅπαντες
ἀθάνατοι φοβέουσι, τοὶ οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι,
sentences.tr:
hossaki d’ hormēseie podarkēs dios Achilleus
stēnai enantibion kai gnōmenai ei min hapantes
athanatoi phobeousi, toi ouranon euryn echousi,
sentences.l:
And as often as swift-footed, heavenly Achilles tried
to stand head-on and to know whether all the immortals
are putting him to flight, who hold the wide heaven,
sentences.i: And as often as swift-footed, heavenly Achilles made a rush to stand against it head-on, and to learn whether all the immortals who hold the wide heaven were putting him to flight,
sentences.n: ὁσσάκι … τοσσάκι (‘as often … so often’) join this unit to the next. ὁρμήσειε is an optative for a repeated action in the past, ‘each time he rushed’. ποδάρκης δῖος Ἀχιλλεύς is ‘swift-footed, heavenly Achilles’; ποδάρκης is a stock epithet whose formation is uncertain. στῆναι ἐναντίβιον is ‘to stand head-on’, with the opponent (the river) understood. γνώμεναι is the infinitive of γιγνώσκω ‘know’, in the epic form in -μεναι. εἰ … φοβέουσι is ‘whether they are putting him to flight’; ἅπαντες ἀθάνατοι is ‘all the immortals’. τοί is the relative ‘who’, and οὐρανὸν εὐρὺν ἔχουσι ‘hold the wide heaven’. The unit ends at a comma, since the sentence would otherwise run past four lines.

sentences.t:
τοσσάκι μιν μέγα κῦμα διιπετέος ποταμοῖο
πλάζ’ ὤμους καθύπερθεν·
sentences.tr:
tossaki min mega kyma diipeteos potamoio
plaz’ ōmous kathyperthen·
sentences.l:
so often him the great wave of the Zeus-fallen river
beat on the shoulders from above;
sentences.i: so often the great wave of the river fallen from Zeus beat upon his shoulders from above;
sentences.n: τοσσάκι is the answer to ὁσσάκι ‘as often’. μιν is Achilles, and ὤμους καθύπερθεν is ‘on the shoulders from above’. πλάζ’ is the imperfect of πλάζω ‘beat, drive back’ without augment and with the final vowel elided. διιπετέος ποταμοῖο is ‘of the river fallen from Zeus’; the word διιπετής is explained as ‘fallen from Zeus’, hence ‘fed by rain’, but its meaning is not certain. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 269.

sentences.t:
ὃ δ’ ὑψόσε ποσσὶν ἐπήδα
θυμῷ ἀνιάζων·
sentences.tr:
ho d’ hypsose possin epēda
thymōi aniazōn·
sentences.l:
and he, upward, with his feet leapt,
in spirit vexed;
sentences.i: and he leapt high with his feet, vexed in spirit;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 269. ὑψόσε is ‘upward, high’, and ἐπήδα is the imperfect of πηδάω ‘leap’, so Achilles keeps trying to clear the wave. ποσσὶν is the epic dative plural of πούς. θυμῷ ἀνιάζων is ‘vexed in spirit’, from ἀνιάζω ‘vex, distress’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 270.

sentences.t:
ποταμὸς δ’ ὑπὸ γούνατ’ ἐδάμνα
λάβρος ὕπαιθα ῥέων, κονίην δ’ ὑπέρεπτε ποδοῖιν.
sentences.tr:
potamos d’ hypo gounat’ edamna
labros hypaitha rheōn, koniēn d’ hyperepte podoiin.
sentences.l:
and the river was overpowering his knees from below,
violent, flowing from beneath, and the dust it was gnawing away under his feet.
sentences.i: and the river, rushing violently from beneath, was overpowering his knees and gnawing the dust from under his feet.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 270. ὑπὸ … ἐδάμνα is split (tmesis): ‘was overpowering from below’, with γούνατ’ (γούνατα, ‘knees’) as its object; ἐδάμνα is the imperfect of δάμνημι ‘overpower’. λάβρος is ‘violent’, and ὕπαιθα ῥέων ‘flowing from beneath’. ὑπέρεπτε is an imperfect found only here, so its sense is inferred from its parts and is not certain: ‘was gnawing from beneath’, from ὑπό and ἔρεπτομαι ‘feed on’; it is the stream undermining the ground. κονίην is ‘dust’, here the loose earth, and ποδοῖιν is a form of the genitive and dative of πούς ‘foot’, here ‘from under his feet’.

sentences.t: Πηλεΐδης δ’ ᾤμωξεν ἰδὼν εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν·
sentences.tr: Pēleïdēs d’ ōimōxen idōn eis ouranon euryn·
sentences.l: And Peleus’-son cried out, looking to the wide heaven:
sentences.i: The son of Peleus cried out, looking up at the wide heaven:
sentences.n: ᾤμωξεν is the aorist of οἰμώζω ‘cry out in distress’. ἰδών is the aorist participle of ὁράω, and εἰς οὐρανὸν εὐρύν ‘to the wide heaven’ is the direction of his look; he looks up, to call on Zeus.

sentences.t:
Ζεῦ πάτερ ὡς οὔ τίς με θεῶν ἐλεεινὸν ὑπέστη
ἐκ ποταμοῖο σαῶσαι·
sentences.tr:
Zeu pater hōs ou tis me theōn eleeinon hypestē
ek potamoio saōsai·
sentences.l:
“Father Zeus, how none of the gods undertook, pitiable as I am,
to save me from the river;
sentences.i: “Father Zeus, how none of the gods has undertaken to save me, pitiable as I am, from the river;
sentences.n: Ζεῦ πάτερ is ‘Father Zeus’. ὡς here is exclamatory ‘how’, not a wish, because the verb ὑπέστη is an indicative. ὑπέστη is the aorist of ὑφίσταμαι ‘undertake’, with the infinitive σαῶσαι (aorist of σαόω ‘save’) and μέ as its object. ἐλεεινόν is ‘pitiable’ and agrees with με. θεῶν is a partitive genitive, ‘of the gods’. ἐκ ποταμοῖο is ‘from the river’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 274.

sentences.t: ἔπειτα δὲ καί τι πάθοιμι.
sentences.tr: epeita de kai ti pathoimi.
sentences.l: and then let me suffer even something.
sentences.i: and after that, let me suffer whatever may come.
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 274. ἔπειτα is ‘afterward’. πάθοιμι is an optative with no κε, so it is a wish or a readiness (‘let me’, ‘I am ready to’), not a prediction; καί τι is ‘even something’, which the English renders as ‘whatever may come’. Achilles says that if a god would save him from the river, he will accept whatever follows.

sentences.t:
ἄλλος δ’ οὔ τις μοι τόσον αἴτιος Οὐρανιώνων,
ἀλλὰ φίλη μήτηρ, ἥ με ψεύδεσσιν ἔθελγεν·
sentences.tr:
allos d’ ou tis moi toson aitios Ouraniōnōn,
alla philē mētēr, hē me pseudessin ethelgen·
sentences.l:
And no other of the sons of Uranus is so much to blame to me,
but my dear mother, who with lies charmed me;
sentences.i: No other of the sons of Uranus is so much to blame as my dear mother, who beguiled me with lies;
sentences.n: ἄλλος δ’ οὔ τις μοι … ἀλλὰ φίλη μήτηρ is ‘no other … but my dear mother’. μοι is ‘to me’, a dative of reference. τόσον αἴτιος is ‘so much to blame’. Οὐρανιώνων is a genitive of Οὐρανίωνες ‘sons of Uranus (Heaven)’; the word is usually understood as the Titans, and the text does not say which gods Achilles means. ψεύδεσσιν is the epic dative plural of ψεῦδος ‘lie’. ἔθελγεν is the imperfect of θέλγω ‘charm, beguile’.

sentences.t:
ἥ μ’ ἔφατο Τρώων ὑπὸ τείχεϊ θωρηκτάων
λαιψηροῖς ὀλέεσθαι Ἀπόλλωνος βελέεσσιν.
sentences.tr:
hē m’ ephato Trōōn hypo teicheï thōrēktaōn
laipsērois oleesthai Apollōnos beleessin.
sentences.l:
who said that I would perish beneath the wall of the Trojans, the corseleted,
by the quick shafts of Apollo.
sentences.i: She told me that I would perish under the wall of the corseleted Trojans, by the quick shafts of Apollo.
sentences.n: ἥ is the relative ‘who’, Achilles’ mother. ἔφατο is a middle imperfect of φημί, ‘said’, with the accusative μ’ and the future infinitive ὀλέεσθαι (Attic ἀπολεῖσθαι) ‘would perish’. Τρώων … θωρηκτάων is ‘of the corseleted Trojans’, from θώραξ ‘corselet’, and ὑπὸ τείχεϊ is ‘under the wall’. λαιψηροῖς … βελέεσσιν is ‘by quick shafts’, with the epic dative plural -εσσιν of βέλος.

sentences.t: ὥς μ’ ὄφελ’ Ἕκτωρ κτεῖναι ὃς ἐνθάδε γ’ ἔτραφ’ ἄριστος·
sentences.tr: hōs m’ ophel’ Hektōr kteinai hos enthade g’ etraph’ aristos·
sentences.l: If only Hector had killed me, who was raised here the best;
sentences.i: If only Hector had killed me, the best man raised here;
sentences.n: ὥς μ’ ὄφελ’ Ἕκτωρ κτεῖναι is a wish about the past, ‘would that Hector had killed me’: ὄφελε is the unaugmented aorist of ὀφείλω ‘ought’ with an infinitive, and ὥς is ‘so’. ὃς ἐνθάδε γ’ ἔτραφ’ ἄριστος is ‘who was raised here as the best’. ἔτραφε is the intransitive aorist of τρέφω ‘grew up’, and ἐνθάδε ‘here’ means in Troy.

sentences.t: τώ κ’ ἀγαθὸς μὲν ἔπεφν’, ἀγαθὸν δέ κεν ἐξενάριξε·
sentences.tr: tō k’ agathos men epephn’, agathon de ken exenarixe·
sentences.l: Then a good man would have killed, and a good man he would have despoiled;
sentences.i: Then a good man would have killed, and a good man he would have stripped of his armour;
sentences.n: τώ is ‘then, in that case’. ἔπεφν’ is the aorist of φένω ‘kill’, and ἐξενάριξε the aorist of ἐξεναρίζω ‘strip a slain man of his arms’, ἔπεφνε being a reduplicated aorist with no augment; κεν goes with both. ἀγαθός is ‘good’ in the sense of ‘brave’: the nominative ἀγαθός is the killer, and the accusative ἀγαθόν is the man he would kill and strip.

sentences.t:
νῦν δέ με λευγαλέῳ θανάτῳ εἵμαρτο ἁλῶναι
ἐρχθέντ’ ἐν μεγάλῳ ποταμῷ ὡς παῖδα συφορβόν,
ὅν ῥά τ’ ἔναυλος ἀποέρσῃ χειμῶνι περῶντα.
sentences.tr:
nyn de me leugaleōi thanatōi heimarto halōnai
erchthent’ en megalōi potamōi hōs paida syphorbon,
hon rha t’ enaulos apoersēi cheimōni perōnta.
sentences.l:
But now it was allotted for me to be caught by a pitiful death,
shut in in a great river like a boy, a swineherd,
whom a torrent sweeps away as he crosses in winter.”
sentences.i: But as it is, it was my lot to be caught by a pitiful death, shut in by a great river like a swineherd’s boy, whom a torrent sweeps away as he crosses in winter.”
sentences.n: The first line of the unit stands at 5.312 of the Odyssey, and its English comes from there. εἵμαρτο is the pluperfect passive of μείρομαι, used impersonally: ‘it was fated’, with the accusative με and the infinitive ἁλῶναι (‘to be caught’). ἐρχθέντ’ is the aorist passive participle of ἔργω ‘shut in’. παῖδα συφορβόν is ‘a boy, a swineherd’. ἔναυλος is a torrent or gully, and ἀποέρσῃ a rare aorist subjunctive meaning ‘sweeps away’. The line is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short syllable πο of ἀποέρσῃ has to count as long, in the first place of the third foot. περῶντα ‘as he crosses’ agrees with ὅν. The speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτο, τῷ δὲ μάλ’ ὦκα Ποσειδάων καὶ Ἀθήνη
στήτην ἐγγὺς ἰόντε, δέμας δ’ ἄνδρεσσιν ἐΐκτην,
χειρὶ δὲ χεῖρα λαβόντες ἐπιστώσαντ’ ἐπέεσσι.
sentences.tr:
hōs phato, tōi de mal’ ōka Poseidaōn kai Athēnē
stētēn engys ionte, demas d’ andressin eïktēn,
cheiri de cheira labontes epistōsant’ epeessi.
sentences.l:
So he spoke, and to him very quickly Poseidon and Athena
stood, coming near, and in build to men were likened,
and taking him hand by hand they pledged him with words.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and very quickly Poseidon and Athena came near and stood by him, in the build of men, and, clasping his hand, they made their pledge to him in words.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο is ‘so he spoke’. The gods are two, and the Greek uses the dual: στήτην ‘the two stood’, ἰόντε ‘the two coming’, ἐΐκτην ‘the two were likened’; τῷ is ‘to him’, Achilles. δέμας is an accusative of respect, ‘in build’, and ἄνδρεσσιν the epic dative plural of ἀνήρ. χειρὶ δὲ χεῖρα λαβόντες is ‘taking hand with hand’, a handclasp. ἐπιστώσαντο is the aorist middle of ἐπιστόω ‘make sure, pledge’, here ‘gave him assurance’, and ἐπέεσσι is ‘with words’.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche Poseidaōn enosichthōn·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning Poseidon earth-shaker:
sentences.i: Poseidon earth-shaker was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: τοῖσι is ‘among them’, the three, and ἦρχε μύθων ‘began the speeches’ means ‘was the first to speak’, with the genitive μύθων. Ποσειδάων ἐνοσίχθων is ‘Poseidon earth-shaker’, his stock epithet. This line stands word for word at 7.445, and its English comes from there.

sentences.t: Πηλεΐδη μήτ’ ἄρ τι λίην τρέε μήτέ τι τάρβει·
sentences.tr: Pēleïdē mēt’ ar ti liēn tree mēte ti tarbei·
sentences.l: “Peleus’-son, neither tremble at all too much, nor be afraid;
sentences.i: “Son of Peleus, do not tremble overmuch, nor be afraid;
sentences.n: Πηλεΐδη is the vocative of Πηλεΐδης ‘son of Peleus’. μήτ’ ἄρ τι λίην τρέε μήτέ τι τάρβει is two prohibitions with μήτε … μήτε in the present imperative: τρέε from τρέω ‘tremble’, τάρβει from ταρβέω ‘be afraid’. λίην is ‘too much’, and ἄρ is the weak particle ἄρα, ‘then’.

sentences.t:
τοίω γάρ τοι νῶϊ θεῶν ἐπιταρρόθω εἰμὲν
Ζηνὸς ἐπαινήσαντος ἐγὼ καὶ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη·
sentences.tr:
toiō gar toi nōï theōn epitarrothō eimen
Zēnos epainēsantos egō kai Pallas Athēnē·
sentences.l:
for such helpers to you of the gods are we two,
Zeus approving, I and Pallas Athena;
sentences.i: for we two are such helpers for you among the gods, with Zeus approving, I and Pallas Athena;
sentences.n: The Greek here uses duals: τοίω ‘such’, νῶϊ ‘we two’ and ἐπιταρρόθω ‘helpers’ (ἐπιτάρροθος, ‘one who rushes to help’, a rare word). τοι is ‘to you’, and θεῶν ‘among the gods’ is partitive. εἰμὲν is the epic form of εἰμέν (Attic ἐσμέν), ‘we are’. Ζηνὸς ἐπαινήσαντος is a genitive absolute, ‘Zeus approving’, with the Homeric form Ζηνός of Zeus’ name. Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη is ‘Pallas Athena’.

sentences.t:
ὡς οὔ τοι ποταμῷ γε δαμήμεναι αἴσιμόν ἐστιν,
ἀλλ’ ὅδε μὲν τάχα λωφήσει, σὺ δὲ εἴσεαι αὐτός·
sentences.tr:
hōs ou toi potamōi ge damēmenai aisimon estin,
all’ hode men tacha lōphēsei, sy de eiseai autos·
sentences.l:
so it is not fitting for you to be overcome by a river,
but this one will soon abate, and you will know it yourself;
sentences.i: so it is not fitting for you to be overcome by a river; he will soon abate, and you will see that for yourself;
sentences.n: ὡς here is ‘so, thus’, drawing the consequence from the last unit. αἴσιμον is ‘fitting’, from αἶσα ‘portion, due’, so the word carries the sense of what is ordained; δαμήμεναι is the aorist passive infinitive of δαμάζω, epic -ήμεναι (Attic δαμῆναι). ὅδε is ‘this one’, the river. λωφήσει is the future of λωφάω ‘abate, take rest’, and εἴσεαι the future of οἶδα ‘you will know’; αὐτός is ‘yourself’.

sentences.t: αὐτάρ τοι πυκινῶς ὑποθησόμεθ’ αἴ κε πίθηαι·
sentences.tr: autar toi pykinōs hypothēsometh’ ai ke pithēai·
sentences.l: but we will suggest to you shrewdly if you will obey;
sentences.i: but we will make shrewd suggestions to you, if you will obey;
sentences.n: αὐτάρ is ‘but’. ὑποθησόμεθ’ is the future middle of ὑποτίθημι ‘suggest’, and the plural is the two gods speaking. πυκινῶς is the adverb of πυκινός and here means ‘shrewdly’. αἴ κε πίθηαι is ‘if you will obey’, with αἰ the epic form of εἰ and πίθηαι the aorist subjunctive middle of πείθω; the verb is in the middle (‘be persuaded’).

sentences.t:
μὴ πρὶν παύειν χεῖρας ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο
πρὶν κατὰ Ἰλιόφι κλυτὰ τείχεα λαὸν ἐέλσαι
Τρωϊκόν, ὅς κε φύγῃσι·
sentences.tr:
mē prin pauein cheiras homoiïou polemoio
prin kata Iliophi klyta teichea laon eelsai
Trōïkon, hos ke phygēisi·
sentences.i: do not stop your hands from the war that is common to all until you have hemmed in the Trojan army within the famous walls of Ilios, whoever of them escapes;
sentences.n: μὴ … παύειν is an infinitive used as a command, ‘do not stop’; πρίν is repeated, ‘not before … before’. ὁμοιΐου πολέμοιο is ‘the war that is common to all’, with ὁμοίϊος ‘common to all, shared’. Ἰλιόφι is Ἴλιος with the suffix -φι (here ‘of Ilios’), and κατά … τείχεα is ‘within the walls’. ἐέλσαι is the aorist infinitive of εἴλω ‘hem in’, with λαὸν … Τρωϊκόν ‘the Trojan people’ as its object. ὅς κε φύγῃσι is ‘whoever escapes’, an aorist subjunctive. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 296.

sentences.t:
σὺ δ’ Ἕκτορι θυμὸν ἀπούρας
ἂψ ἐπὶ νῆας ἴμεν·
sentences.tr:
sy d’ Hektori thymon apouras
aps epi nēas imen·
sentences.l:
and you, having taken Hector’s life away,
back to the ships go;
sentences.i: and when you have taken Hector’s life, go back to the ships;
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 296. σύ δ’ is ‘and you’. Ἕκτορι is a dative of disadvantage, so θυμὸν ἀπούρας is ‘having taken the life from Hector’; ἀπούρας is the aorist participle of ἀπαυράω ‘take away’. ἂψ ἐπὶ νῆας ἴμεν is ‘back to the ships’, where ἴμεν is an infinitive used as a command, ‘go’. The unit ends at the ano teleia in the middle of line 297.

sentences.t: δίδομεν δέ τοι εὖχος ἀρέσθαι.
sentences.tr: didomen de toi euchos aresthai.
sentences.l: we give you to win a boast.”
sentences.i: and we grant you to win the triumph.”
sentences.n: The unit begins in the middle of line 297. δίδομεν is ‘we give’, the two gods promising, and τοι is ‘to you’. εὖχος is ‘a boast, a vaunt’, and so ‘the triumph’ over which one boasts. ἀρέσθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of αἴρομαι, ‘to win’. The speech ends here.
